/food/.title: Nigerian Menu | Nourish Sahel
/food/.main:
Our kitchen menu

Explore our first dishes and our Hibiscus and Ginger drink. For ingredients, serving sizes or availability, get in touch.

Heritage Fonio Jollof

Acha takes on the deep flavour of tomato and pepper. Grilled guinea fowl brings a smoky edge, with pumpkin greens alongside.

Tilapia and Uziza Broth

Ginger, uziza and scent leaf give this pepper broth its fragrance. Tilapia is the centre of the bowl, with tender pieces of plantain.

Steamed Cowpea Cakes

Peeled cowpeas, red pepper and herbs are gently steamed into soft cakes. A spoonful of tiger-nut cream brings a smooth finish.

Smoked Beef and Millet

Smoked beef brings depth to a slow tomato stew finished with scent leaf. Warm millet couscous soaks up the sauce.

Hibiscus and Ginger

Hibiscus gives this chilled drink its ruby colour. Ginger adds brightness, cloves and cinnamon add warmth, and dates give it a little sweetness.

The Nourish Sahel approach

How we build a plate

  • Give greens and beans room.

    We serve our fonio jollof with pumpkin greens and make our steamed cakes with cowpeas.

  • Choose the grain for the dish.

    Acha takes on our tomato and pepper base. Millet holds its own alongside a smoky stew.

  • Build flavour in the pot.

    We use ginger, scent leaf, peppers and other aromatics, and cook without added MSG.

/about/our-story/.title: Our Story | Nourish Sahel
/about/our-story/.main:
Eat well. Keep the flavours you love.

How can we eat healthier and still enjoy the Nigerian food we grew up with?

Healthy eating for everyday life.

We’d still give the stew time for the tomatoes and peppers to deepen. We’d still simmer tilapia with ginger and scent leaf. We’d make more room on the plate for vegetables and beans, and give grains like millet, sorghum and acha a place in the meals we already love.

Nourish Sahel is a Nigerian food company. We share practical food guides, prepare healthier everyday meals in our Abuja kitchen, and are building FitTrac to help you plan your meals.

We cook without added MSG.

/about/how-we-cook/.title: How We Cook | Nourish Sahel
/about/how-we-cook/.main:
Flavour starts with what goes into the pot.

We cook tomatoes until their flavour deepens. We give ginger, pepper and scent leaf time to come through in a broth.

We cook with measured oil and less salt, without seasoning cubes or added MSG.

We start with the vegetables, beans or proteins that suit the dish, then choose the grain or other side to serve alongside.

/about/our-commitments/.title: Our Commitments | Nourish Sahel
/about/our-commitments/.main:
What goes on the plate matters.

More room for vegetables and beans. More variety beyond rice. Flavour from the ingredients.

Vegetables and beans

Greens, cowpeas and other vegetables and legumes help shape the meal from the start.

Grain variety

We use grains such as millet, sorghum and acha where they suit the dish, and give vegetables and proteins more space on the plate.

Kitchen craft

We cook with herbs, spices, peppers and aromatics, without added MSG.

/faq/.main:
Questions about Nourish Sahel

About our first menu, ingredients and workplace meals.

Can I order now?

We’re preparing our first menu and will share ordering details when they’re available.

What grains do you use?

Our first menu concepts include acha and millet. We’re also exploring sorghum.

Do you cook with added MSG?

We cook without added MSG. We use herbs, spices, peppers and aromatics to build flavour.

Where can I check ingredients and allergens?

We’ll publish ingredient and allergen information with the menu before ordering opens.

Can I arrange lunch for my team?

Tell us your location, team size and what you have in mind.

/journal/grain-variety/.title: What a grain brings to the plate | Nourish Sahel
/journal/grain-variety/.main:
What a grain brings to the plate

Ingredients

Acha, millet and sorghum each change the way a meal tastes and feels. The best choice starts with what else is on the plate.

Start with what you want to cook

In jollof, fine acha grains take on the tomato and pepper base in little spoonfuls. With a stew, we might reach for millet. Its fuller texture gives the sauce something to cling to and holds its own alongside smoked beef and scent leaf. Sorghum gives us another grain to explore as the menu develops.

Give the rest of the plate equal attention

Changing the grain is only one decision. With our acha jollof, grilled guinea fowl brings a smoky edge and pumpkin greens bring a different texture. In other dishes, beans or fish may take the lead. We decide how much space each part needs once we know what it contributes.

Build variety into the week

A grain you enjoy on Monday doesn’t have to carry the whole week. We want the menu to make room for a bowl of jollof, a ginger-scented broth, and a meal built around cowpeas. Each one is satisfying in a different way.

/journal/where-flavour-begins/.title: Where the flavour begins | Nourish Sahel
/journal/where-flavour-begins/.main:
Where the flavour begins

In the kitchen

A pot of pepper broth and a slow tomato stew show how timing, heat and familiar ingredients build flavour in the Nourish Sahel kitchen.

Give the broth time

When we build a tilapia broth, ginger and pepper go in early so their flavour can move through the pot. Uziza brings its own character, while scent leaf gives the finished broth the fragrance you notice as you lean over the bowl. The fish needs its own timing, so it can stay tender.

Cook the base until it tastes ready

A tomato stew changes as it cooks. The tomatoes lose their raw edge and the pepper settles into the sauce. The cook tastes as it goes, because the point at which a base is ready depends on the ingredients in the pot that day. Smoked beef adds a savoury depth of its own.

Make flavour part of the recipe

We cook without added MSG. The way we prepare the dish matters as much as the list of ingredients. Steaming the cowpea cakes gives them a soft texture. Grilling the guinea fowl brings a little char. Those are choices you can taste when you sit down to eat.

/journal/lunch-break/.title: A lunch break worth keeping | Nourish Sahel
/journal/lunch-break/.main:
A lunch break worth keeping

Everyday eating

The meal you want on a rushed Tuesday might be different from what you want later in the week. We’re designing our plans around that.

Choose for the day you actually have

A bowl of tilapia broth might suit a day when you can sit down with a spoon. Steamed cowpea cakes or a bowl of acha jollof might be what you’re looking forward to on another day. The useful question is which meal you’ll be glad to see when lunchtime comes.

Make the next decision easier

Planning a few lunches ahead gives you space to choose while you still have time to think. We’re developing a rotating menu around vegetables, beans, proteins and a variety of grains, so the week can include meals with different textures and flavours.

See the week in one place

That’s the idea behind FitTrac, the app we’re building for Nourish Sahel. The planned experience lets you choose meals for the days that suit you and see your delivery details in one place. We’ll share more as the app and meal plans take shape.

/journal/build-the-plate/.title: How We Build a Nourish Sahel Plate | Nourish Sahel
/journal/build-the-plate/.main:
How we build a Nourish Sahel plate

Our approach

When rice is usually the starting point, it’s easy for the rest of the meal to feel like a side. Here’s how we make room for more variety.

Start with what gives the dish its character

For tilapia and uziza broth, the starting point is the fish and the fragrant broth. For our steamed cakes, it’s the cowpeas and red pepper. That choice gives the dish its identity before we decide which grain or other side belongs with it.

Give the vegetables a job

Pumpkin greens bring a different texture to acha jollof and sit well with the smoky flavour of grilled guinea fowl. Scent leaf is part of what makes a smoked beef stew recognisable. We think about what each ingredient contributes before deciding how much of it belongs in the meal.

Choose a side that works with the dish

Millet sits well next to a stew. Tender plantain makes sense in a broth. Acha can carry the tomato and pepper flavours of jollof. Some meals begin with beans and have a different balance altogether. The goal is a plate you look forward to eating, with more room for the ingredients that make it good.

/food-guides/.main:
Food guides

Practical ideas for healthier everyday Nigerian meals.

Soups and everyday meals

Try Afang with fish and boiled unripe plantain, efo riro with roasted sweet potatoes, or miyan taushe with millet. Serve moi moi with greens or spoon tomato and pepper stew over acha.

Nigerian salad and coleslaw

Start with cabbage, carrots, cucumber, lettuce and tomatoes. Add boiled eggs, grilled chicken or fish if you like.

For a creamy salad, use plain, unsweetened Greek yoghurt instead of mayonnaise. Season with lime, garlic and black pepper. For a plant-based salad, try lime, ginger and fresh herbs. Neither dressing needs added sugar.

Eating with a specific need in mind?

If you’re following dietary advice, use the ingredients, preparation and serving ideas to see what fits the guidance you’ve been given.
